extracted.intended_audience: educated early-18th-century London readers: theatregoers, actors, writers, and moral critics
extracted.subtask_description: Short moral and critical essays addressing theatrical taste, social behaviour, and the ethics of satire and reputation; includes guidance for representation on stage (madness, passion), conduct (impudence, envy), and proper use of wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of human life in plays
rubrics_metrics.description: Plays should concern human life and be a picture of Nature; entertainments ought to engage the Understanding rather than rely on improbable or monstrous inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise is given when a play reflects 'human Life' and natural motives; anti-patterns include 'improbable, monstrous, and incoherent Dreams' that provoke applause from 'Idiots' rather than genuine admiration. Present letters from players criticizing current taste as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility and coherence of theatrical spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Stage works should avoid incoherence and improbability; spectators should be able to recognise human motives rather than be amused by extravagant, unbelievable effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid scenes whose events or character behaviour are so unlikely they exclude the audience's reason. The essay condemns the Town's applause for 'monstrous things' and 'incoherent Dreams'—use plausible action and coherent cause-and-effect in plotting and staging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of madness as disturbance of a noble mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Madness, when staged, should arise from the disturbance of a noble or generous mind (e.g., grief, humane resentments) rather than be reduced to base appetites or comic mannerisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good examples: Shakespeare's noble madness grounded in humane passions; anti-patterns: scenes that represent madness as mere lust or thirst (an 'Idiots' scene), or comic drunkenness presented as true madness. Actors and writers should aim for humane, psychologically-grounded depictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting requires understanding and truthful passion
rubrics_metrics.description: To play justly requires a degree of understanding and the capacity to represent passions truthfully rather than resort to mechanical or merely comic effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While actors must sometimes 'suspend their Reason' to inhabit parts, the best acting springs from comprehension of motive and feeling. Anti-patterns include performances that reduce parts to mechanical appetite or inanimate poses (e.g., actors reduced to hangings, chairs, or flower-pots).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical use of wit and satire (avoid private, vindictive lampoons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire and lampooning, even when clever, become morally harmful when used to wound private persons and family reputations; ill-natured wit that targets the innocent is condemnable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay likens well-written lampoons to 'poison'd Darts' that make wounds incurable; guidance is to avoid anonymous or malicious ridicule of individuals and 'raise Uneasiness among near Relations'. Prefer satire that addresses vice or public faults rather than private reputations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding provocation of Envy when one gains reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who acquire fame should temper their behaviour and appearance to avoid inflaming envy in others; modesty and occasional self-deprecation can relieve the pains of envious readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the author deliberately exposes his own unhandsome face after praise to lessen others' envy. Anti-pattern: ostentation or continual self-promotion that increases others' distress and malignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedying social impudence (behavioural correction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Impudence—especially the impertinent staring that disturbs public worship or gatherings—should be corrected not by mere reasoned admonition (which often fails) but by social response and confrontation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical remedy offered: confront the stare (e.g., a defender to 'stare against him'), place oneself to meet his eyes so he feels shame. Description includes national varieties of impudence as comic material but insists true impudence merits blame, not jocular celebration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatre should reward merit and not reduce performers to spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: A just theatre rewards performers according to merit; it is a fault of the stage and audience to elevate inanity or novelty while neglecting genuine talent, reducing some actors to motionless or prop-like roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Letters from stage-hands (flower-pots, hangings, chairs) are cited to show how merit is overlooked. Guidance: managers and audiences should recognize and promote true ability rather than favour spectacle or novelty at the expense of deserving performers.
